name: Handheld camera
summary: A camera that the operator carries on the body, with no tripod or dolly; the shake of the body shows in the frame.
how: Use a light camera and a wide lens of 18mm to 35mm so that the shake stays small in the frame.
Follow the action at the pace of a walking person and let the frame move 2% to 5% off the subject.
Do not stabilise in post; accept a late refocus and a missed frame as part of the take.
Shoot long takes of 30 seconds or more, so that the camera seems to live in the room.

origin.note: Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin shoot Chronique d'un été with the light synchronous-sound camera that Michel Brault operates by hand; earlier handheld shots exist.

adoptions.via: Raoul Coutard shoots À bout de souffle by hand for Jean-Luc Godard.
Rouch, Brault and the Direct Cinema crews carry the light 16mm camera and the sound recorder into real rooms.
Easy Rider and other New Hollywood films use light cameras on real roads and locations.
The Dogme 95 Vow of Chastity demands that the camera is hand-held.
The Blair Witch Project gives the camera to its characters and shows the shake as their fear.
Andrew Bujalski shoots Funny Ha Ha with a small camera in plain rooms.
Sean Baker shoots Tangerine on three iPhone 5S phones with a clip-on anamorphic lens and a small stabiliser.
Camcorder revival films shoot on handheld consumer video cameras.

sources.title: Richard Neupert, A History of the French New Wave Cinema (University of Wisconsin Press, 2002)
